clue.text: Short line for character is inspiring? Just the reverse

indicators.note: the clue's own words tell the solver to turn the preceding phrase back to front

parts.note: to inspire someone is to fire them up, so 'is inspiring' gives fires

explanation.surface: Someone muses that a short line in a play is inspiring for its character, then decides the opposite is true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just the reverse' turns FIRES (from 'is inspiring') round to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A serif is the small stroke finishing off a printed letter, so it is a short line on a typeface character.

clue.text: Sheepish type is a point behind

parts.note: south is one of the points of the compass
a team that is behind in a game is down

explanation.surface: A timid person trails by one point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheepish' suggests shyness, but means a type of sheep: the Southdown is an English breed from the South Downs hills.
explanation.definitionFit: The Southdown is a breed of sheep, so it is literally an ovine type.

clue.text: Switch on at home for sculptor's appearance

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece set on another stands above it

parts.note: a switch is a thin rod or cane
in means at home

explanation.surface: Turning on the lights at home ahead of a visit from an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switch on' looks like a light switch; a switch is a cane, sitting on top of IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Auguste Rodin was the French sculptor of The Thinker.

clue.text: One novelist or another who's written about English

indicators.note: the other novelist's name is written around the English letter

parts.note: another novelist, E. M. Forster, author of A Passage to India

explanation.surface: Two novelists, one of whom writes about Englishness.
explanation.definitionFit: C. S. Forester wrote the Hornblower novels.

clue.text: Pieces of bread set outside as food for birds

indicators.note: the word for set is placed on the outside of the other piece

parts.note: jelly that has set has gelled, so set gives gel
rounds are slices of bread, as in a round of toast

explanation.surface: Bits of bread put out on the bird table.
explanation.definitionFit: Groundsel is a common weed whose seeds are fed to cage birds, so it is bird food.

clue.text: Vehemently attack lecher

explanation.surface: Lay into a womaniser.
explanation.definitionFit: To go at someone is to set about them fiercely; a lustful man is called a randy old billy, a lecher.

clue.text: Traditional number, unlike 6

explanation.surface: A familiar song that differs from another clue's answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 is NEWTON, read as NEW TON; its opposite is old (not new) hundred (a ton is a hundred).
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Hundredth is a traditional hymn tune, a number in a hymnbook; and old hundred reverses new ton term for term.

clue.text: Scientist producing element without weight

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the element surrounds the weight

parts.note: neon is a chemical element

explanation.surface: A researcher isolates an element that has no weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' seems to mean lacking, but here means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Newton was the physicist who described gravity.

clue.text: Game of cards that might be rummy is lost — how?

indicators.note: rummy means odd or strange, so the letters may be shuffled oddly

explanation.surface: A card game turning out to be rummy, and a puzzled 'how did I lose?'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rummy' looks like the card game; here it means peculiar, signalling the anagram of IS LOST HOW.
explanation.definitionFit: Solo whist is a trick-taking card game for four in which players may bid to play alone.

clue.text: Hard-hearted humorist or composer

indicators.note: the hard letter is placed at the heart of the humorist's name

parts.note: Edward Lear wrote nonsense verse and limericks
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A stern comic writer or a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard-hearted' reads as callous, but splits into H at the heart of LEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Lehár wrote the operetta The Merry Widow.

clue.text: Figure on clock may be so crooked

definitions.text: Figure on clock may be so

explanation.surface: A dial figure drawn askew.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: each numeral on a clock face sits beneath a hand at some moment, so it may be under a hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A numeral lies below a hand of the clock; and underhand dealing is crooked, dishonest and secret.

clue.text: People out West refuse to become settlers

explanation.surface: Westerners decline to put down roots.
explanation.walkthrough: Wales lies west of England. 'Settlers' is not colonists but people who settle a bill: to welsh is to dodge paying a debt, such as a bet.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of Wales live to Britain's west; and to welsh on a wager is to fail to pay up.

clue.text: Just a little house, a cosy home

parts.note: HO is a standard abbreviation for house, so a shortened house
a nest is a snug home, as in a love nest

explanation.surface: A description of a small house as nothing more than a snug home.
explanation.definitionFit: A just person is fair and truthful, synonyms for upright.

clue.text: Vessel in conflict? Struggle with anchors at both ends

definitions.text: Struggle with anchors at both ends

explanation.surface: A boat in a battle, or a contest with weights at each end.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is whimsical: a small towing boat caught up in war. The 'anchors' are the heaviest team members placed at the rope's end.
explanation.definitionFit: A tug is a towing boat and war a conflict; the rope-pulling contest has an anchor at each team's back end.

clue.text: Party speeches in place of careful analysis

parts.note: Lab is the short form of the Labour Party
oratory is the art of public speaking, or speeches collectively

explanation.surface: Political speeches stand in for careful scrutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: A laboratory is a room where scientists carry out tests and experiments.

clue.text: How some gamblers bet, with quite high probability

explanation.surface: Gamblers backing a card game with good odds.
explanation.definitionFit: A card player stakes money on what the cards show; an outcome that is likely is said to be in prospect, the same idiom.

clue.text: Lack of originality and interest's awful

indicators.note: something awful is in a bad state, so the letters are mangled

parts.note: the word and its s are the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Complaining that something is unoriginal and dreadfully dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Triteness is staleness, the quality of being hackneyed.

clue.text: Row in boat if fit

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters across 'boat if fit'

explanation.surface: Someone says they will row in the boat if they are fit enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like the oarsman's verb but is the noun rhyming with cow, a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiff is a minor quarrel, the sense of row as a squabble.

clue.text: Vessel French crew joined with hesitation

parts.note: a rowing eight is a crew
er is the sound of hesitating

explanation.surface: A French crew boards a ship, after some hesitation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crew' suggests sailors but is the rowing crew of eight.
explanation.definitionFit: A freighter is a cargo ship.

clue.text: Display document for 17

explanation.surface: Show the paperwork for another clue's answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 is the cargo ship, which carries a list of its cargo.
explanation.definitionFit: To manifest is to show plainly; a ship's manifest lists the cargo a cargo vessel carries.

clue.text: It may be beautifully painted, but it shouldn't come under the hammer

definitions.text: It may be beautifully painted, but it shouldn't come under the hammer

parts.words: It may be beautifully painted, but it shouldn't come under the hammer
parts.note: the surface suggests an artwork that ought not to be auctioned, but read literally it is something manicured and lacquered that a carpenter must not strike

explanation.surface: A fine painting that should never be sold at auction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under the hammer' means sold at auction, but here it is literal: the fingertip part you paint must not be hit when hammering one into wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Fingernails are painted with varnish, and when hammering a metal spike the finger holding it must avoid the hammer.

clue.text: Warning man on board this part of ship's for quarters

definitions.text: this part of ship's for quarters

parts.note: golfers shout fore as a warning
a castle (rook) is a chess man on the board

explanation.surface: A warning shouted to a crewman about his billet aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man on board' suggests a sailor but means a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The forecastle, at the bow, is where the crew's sleeping quarters were traditionally housed.

clue.text: Ancient weapon

explanation.surface: An old gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient' looks like 'old', but is the old military rank of ensign: Ancient Pistol is a Shakespeare character in Henry IV and Henry V.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Pistol holds the rank of ancient (ensign); a pistol is a handgun.

clue.text: Union leader, politician and dramatist

explanation.surface: A trade union boss who is also an MP and a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' is not a trade union: Philip Sheridan was a Union general in the American Civil War. Richard Brinsley Sheridan was both an MP and the author of The Rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Sheridan led Northern cavalry; R. B. Sheridan wrote comedies and sat in Parliament.

clue.text: Founders of new colony finding South hospitable

parts.note: a warm welcome is a hospitable one

explanation.surface: Settlers founding a colony find the south welcoming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Founders of new colony' suggests pioneers, but bees that leave the hive in a swarm found a new colony.
explanation.definitionFit: A swarm of bees leaves the hive with a queen to set up a new nest.

clue.text: Extensive cover-up after capital loss is notable

parts.note: something extensive is big
capital is the head, so losing hair from it leads to a covering hairpiece

explanation.surface: A large cover-up following a financial loss in the capital is noteworthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital loss' looks financial but means loss of hair from the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigwig is an important person, a noted figure; here the noun sense of notable.

clue.text: Be careful in sound — there's a danger to shipping

indicators.note: the word is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to reck is an old verb for to heed or take care

explanation.surface: A warning to take care in the strait, where ships are at risk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like a stretch of sea, but signals a homophone of RECK.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunken hulk is a hazard that ships may run into.

clue.text: Bow that's kind of ordinary

explanation.surface: A bow that is quite plain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordinary' is a heraldic term: the bend is a diagonal band across a shield, one of the ordinaries.
explanation.definitionFit: To bow is to stoop forward; a heraldic bend is one of the simple charges called ordinaries.

clue.text: Claim by originator of tax dodge

parts.note: to aver is to state firmly, to claim

indicators.note: the originator of a word is its starting letter, here of tax

explanation.surface: A claim made by the man who devised a tax-avoidance scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: To avert something is to turn it aside or prevent it, so to sidestep it.

clue.text: It's obvious English king is absorbed in work too much

indicators.note: the English king letters go inside the word for obvious

parts.note: overt means open and obvious
rex is Latin for king, as on coins and documents

explanation.surface: Plainly an English monarch is too absorbed in his work.
explanation.definitionFit: To overexert oneself is to strain beyond one's strength, to overdo it.

clue.text: Drove badly, perhaps, spread out on the motorway

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway north from London, with 1 read as the letter I
splayed means spread out

explanation.surface: A driver who steered poorly, swerving across the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drove' suggests a car, but a golfer's drive is a shot; driving badly is one example of a misplayed stroke, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf drive hit poorly is a shot played wrongly.

clue.text: To capture queen is better, possibly

parts.note: to take a piece is to capture it
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A chess remark that taking the queen is the better move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is not the comparative but one who bets; someone who accepts a wager is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who accepts a bet offered is one kind of gambler.
